newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS - Ord seen as first agri-venture in title test.
newsitem.headline: RTRS - Ord seen as first agri-venture in title test.

text.p: Major expansion at the A$500 million Ord River irrigation scheme in the remote northwest of Western Australia (WA) is being flagged as Australia's first potential major agricultural victim of native title claims.

Expressions of interest will be called in April for the development of an extra 45,000 hectares of land at the Ord River Scheme, with cotton, sugar and other agricultural pursuits expected to dominate.

But Ord phase two tenders will be called just months after Australia's High Court ruled in December that claims by the Wik Aboriginal group over 35,000 square km of Queensland land may in some cases extinguish the rights of pastoral leaseholders.

Native title confusion now poses the latest threat to development at the Ord, which was conceived almost 40 years ago, abandoned 20 years ago mainly because of cotton-destroying insect plagues, then in recent years revived to produce sugar, maize, cotton, fruit and cattle.

"Title will be an issue for any person going in. Any developer will ask 'what title do I have?'" Nick Gill, commercial manager of Colly Cotton Ltd, one of Australia's largest cotton groups, told Reuters.

Colly this week announced it would build an A$800,000 cotton gin at Kununurra as part of the Ord's return to fullscale cotton production. It also said it planned to build a larger gin in 2000 to coincide with the Ord's planned phase two.

Gill told Reuters that the first gin was not threatened by native title confusion. However, the later, bigger cotton gin investment would clearly depend on Ord River phase two going ahead, and that depended on developments in native title.
WA's conservative Premier Richard Court, in his public statements, sees Ord two as clearly under native title threat.

Numerous investment projects in WA had been put at risk by the unworkability of the present legislative regime on native title, including the Ord River Scheme and several tourist developments in both Broome and Kununurra, he said this week.
Gill does not see native title as quite the same threat as premier Court in his public statements.
Native title was mentioned as an issue in documents involved with the tender process for Ord phase two, Gill said. And native title claims in WA extend from Perth airport on, he said.
"It's a matter of patience," he said, adding that the real meaning of native title was probably that a project might end up being more expensive than otherwise would be the case.
But Ord phase two still looked like being the first large agricultural project involved in a native title hold-up or breakthrough, he said.
Phase one of the Ord project involved 14,000 hectares area, with sugar taking 3,000 ha, maize 2,000 ha and cotton 200 ha.
In phase two's 45,000 ha of additional development, cotton and sugar are both expected to take 10,000-12,000 ha.
The gin which Colly Cotton is looking at establishing for phase two could handle up to 14,000 ha, he said.

The Ord is producing its first substantial sugar cane crop in 1996/97, with production at about 40,000 tonnes of raw sugar after CSR Ltd's new A$40 million Ord mill completed its first full crushing year in 1996.
Other projects in Ord phase one include fruit, a 30 megawatt hydro-electric power station, live cattle for export to Asia and hybrid sunflower and sorghum seed production.
